Below is a concise, evidence‑backed definition of “food bioactives,” their scope, mechanisms, and how they relate to nutrients, functional foods, and regulation.

Definition and scope
- Core definition: Food bioactives are constituents of foods—other than those required to meet basic nutritional needs—that have biological activity in humans, producing effects on health status or physiological functions beyond their energy, protein, carbohydrate, vitamin, and mineral roles <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactive compounds in foods are “extra‑nutritional substances that are biologically active and naturally occurring,” associated with changes in health status beyond basic nutrition</cite> <cite id="be6826b9-2">A food bioactive compound is “a compound, mostly without nutritional value and naturally present in food, that is associated with biological activity in the human body”</cite>. 
- Directionality: Bioactivity can be beneficial or adverse; in many contemporary uses, “bioactive” in nutrition is applied to beneficial effects, but negative bioactivity is recognized and relevant for food safety and risk assessment <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactivity can be understood in either a positive or negative sense; within this study, bioactive compounds are defined as those demonstrating beneficial effects, but foods may also contain substances associated with negative health effects</cite>.
- Synonyms and distinctions: The terms “bioactive compounds,” “phytochemicals/phytonutrients,” “nutraceuticals,” and “functional foods” are often used loosely; there is no single international consensus, and clarifying boundaries is essential for both consumers and regulators <cite id="be6826b9-2">Terms such as bioactive compounds, phytochemicals, nutraceuticals, and functional foods frequently appear, yet there is no international consensus on their definitions and boundaries are unclear and often interchangeable</cite>.

Relationship to functional foods and health claims
- Functional foods vs. bioactives: Foods are “products of various origins that contain nutrients, compounds responsible for organoleptic characteristics, and other substances that are associated with positive effects on health independently of their nutritional value,” and those other substances are the bioactives that confer benefits beyond nutrition <cite id="be6826b9-2">Foods contain nutrients and other substances associated with positive effects on health independently of nutritional value; these other substances are the bioactives</cite>. 
- Mechanistic criterion: A food is functional if it “satisfactorily demonstrates” a beneficial effect on one or more target functions in the body beyond adequate nutrition, relevant to improved health or reduced disease risk; EFSA evaluates such effects under Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 via nutrition and health claims, including functional health and disease‑risk‑reduction claims <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">A food can be regarded as functional if it is satisfactorily demonstrated to affect beneficially one or more target functions beyond adequate nutritional effects, relevant to improved health and/or reduced risk of disease</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">EFSA focuses on evaluating health claims (nutrition and health claims regulation 1924/2006); health claims include functional health (Article 13) and disease‑risk‑reduction claims (Article 14)</cite>. 
- Practical definition via regulation: In marketing and policy, bioactive‑driven benefits are communicated through health claims, and authorized claims are managed by EFSA; EU practice emphasizes evidence for physiological effects at typical dietary intake levels <cite id="d1bd4a9e-0">The Health Claims Regulation (EFSA) lists permitted health claims for nutrients, substances, or foods; marketing of possible health effects requires EFSA authorization</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Beneficial effects should occur at intake levels consistent with typical dietary consumption; EFSA evaluates claims under 1924/2006</cite>. 
- Boundary with nutrients: Regulatory and scholarly definitions explicitly exclude basic nutrient sufficiency from “functional” status; benefits must be beyond meeting nutritional needs, aligning bioactives with “other biologically active components” in addition to nutrients <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Institutes’ definitions include foods and components providing health benefits beyond basic nutrition, including other biologically active components</cite> <cite id="be6826b9-2">Frank et al.: bioactive food components are “other than those required to meet basic nutritional needs,” associated with changes in health status</cite>.

Mechanisms, pathways, and typical effects
- Common modes of action: Modulation of inflammation, antioxidant effects, lipid metabolism, and regulation of gene expression; these mechanistic actions are linked to prevention or management of chronic diseases (e.g., type 2 diabetes, cancer) <cite id="be6826b9-2">Roles include modulation of inflammation, antioxidant effects, reducing lipid levels, and regulating gene expression, crucial for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and cancer</cite>. 
- Dose and context: Bioactive effects can occur at low intakes and at defined, effective, non‑toxic doses; contemporary definitions emphasize clinically proven, biomarker‑based benefits at realistic dietary levels rather than “unknown” or undefined compounds <cite id="2faceea1-0">Functional foods contain bioactive compounds with health‑promoting and -protecting properties (antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, antifungal, antimicrobial, antiviral) and can be characterized as functional when their bioactives provide recognizable health benefits</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-1">Functional Food Center definition: foods with biologically active compounds that, in defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts, provide clinically proven, biomarker‑utilizing health benefits for prevention, management, or treatment of chronic disease or symptoms</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-1">An updated FFC definition removes the notion of unknown compounds and acknowledges treating symptoms as well as managing chronic disease</cite>.

What counts as a food bioactive
- Chemical classes and sources: Naturally occurring plant and microbial metabolites (e.g., phenolics, carotenoids, fibers, oligosaccharides, pectins, and bioactive peptides) are typical examples; they are diverse and heterogeneous, with discovery of new molecules ongoing <cite id="2faceea1-0">Bioactive compounds occur naturally as plant and/or microbial metabolites; they are keystones for functional food development, with examples including organic acids, phytochemicals (phenolics, carotenoids), oligosaccharides, pectins, and bioactive peptides</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-4">Bioactive compounds are natural compounds capable of interacting with one or more components of living tissues and exerting a variety of effects; distinctions with dietary supplements, nutraceuticals, and functional foods are sometimes misinterpreted</cite>. 
- Interaction and target specificity: A bioactive is a compound capable of interacting with tissues and altering biological processes, distinguishing it from bulk nutrients by mechanism‑level effects on pathways or biomarkers <cite id="2faceea1-4">Bioactive compounds are natural compounds capable of interacting with one or more components of living tissues and exerting a variety of effects</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">Health claims describe the physiological effects of food components, supported by EFSA</cite>.

Distinctions and cautions
- Avoiding overreach: Not all bioactives are nutrients; not all nutrients are bioactives. Nutrients fulfill nutritional roles and may have physiological effects, but bioactives are specifically “other biologically active components” that deliver benefits beyond meeting nutritional needs at intake levels relevant to typical diets <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Foods and components that provide health benefits beyond basic nutrition, including other biologically active components</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Benefits should occur at intake levels consistent with typical dietary consumption</cite>. 
- Regulatory heterogeneity: Definitions and frameworks vary internationally; EU centers evaluation on EFSA‑authorized health claims, while other jurisdictions (e.g., Japan’s FOSHU and “foods with function claims”) differ, and the U.S. lacks a single coherent regulatory category—underscoring that “bioactive” is best understood via evidence standards (randomized trials, biomarkers, safety) rather than a single legal label <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Various countries have adopted different concepts in terms of definition and regulatory frameworks (bioavailability, clinical effect, permitted nutrition and health claims)</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-0">EU health claims are authorized by EFSA and published in Regulation (EU) No 432/2012</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Japan’s FOSHU and newer “foods with function claims” systems illustrate regulatory diversity</cite>. 
- Scope includes negatives: Foods can contain bioactives with adverse effects; thus, “bioactivity” per se is not synonymous with “beneficial,” and risk–benefit assessment is essential <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactivity can be understood in either a positive or negative sense, with foods sometimes containing substances associated with negative health effects</cite>.

Practical identification and evaluation criteria
- Ask four questions:
  1) Is it present in foods at measurable levels apart from basic nutrients? <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactives are non‑nutritive constituents naturally present in foods</cite>.
  2) Does it show biological activity in humans (e.g., antioxidant capacity, anti‑inflammatory signaling, lipid lowering, gene regulation) at realistic intakes? <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactives modulate inflammation, reduce lipids, regulate gene expression; roles linked to prevention of chronic disease</cite>.
  3) Is the effect linked to specific target functions with biomarker changes and clinically relevant outcomes at defined, effective, non‑toxic doses and typical dietary exposure? <cite id="2faceea1-1">Defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts with clinically proven, biomarker‑utilizing benefits</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Effects should occur at intake levels consistent with typical diet; EFSA evaluates functional and risk‑reduction health claims</cite>.
  4) Is the label evidence‑based and compliant with regulatory health‑claim standards (e.g., EFSA authorization), or at least framed as a plausible, testable mechanism rather than unqualified disease prevention/treatment? <cite id="d1bd4a9e-0">EFSA authorizes health claims; marketing of health effects requires EFSA recommendation</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">EFSA distinguishes function health and disease risk‑reduction claims under 1924/2006</cite>.

Illustrative subdomains
- Phenolics and carotenoids (antioxidants), fibers and prebiotic oligosaccharides/pectins (gut microbiota modulation), and bioactive peptides (biopeptides) are canonical examples, illustrating how structure (molecule class and conformation) enables bioactivity via absorption, metabolism, and interaction with receptors/genes <cite id="2faceea1-0">Phytochemicals (phenolics and carotenoids), oligosaccharides, pectins, and bioactive peptides exemplify functional compounds</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-0">Bioactive compounds are natural plant and microbial metabolites with antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, antifungal, antimicrobial, and antiviral properties</cite>.

Putting it together: a working definition
- In practice, a food bioactive is any non‑nutritive, naturally occurring constituent of foods (and sometimes dietary supplements) that interacts with human tissues or biological systems to produce a measurable, beneficial change in physiological function or disease risk at intakes achievable in normal diets, distinct from the effects required to meet nutritional needs; evaluation relies on mechanistic plausibility, biomarker‑based endpoints, clinical evidence, and safety at defined effective doses, and is framed within regulated health‑claims systems such as EFSA’s in the EU <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactive compounds are extra‑nutritional, naturally occurring substances associated with changes in health status</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-1">Bioactive compounds in defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts provide clinically proven, biomarker‑based health benefits</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">A food is functional if it beneficially affects one or more target functions beyond nutrition</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-0">EFSA authorizes health claims; EU regulation (432/2012) lists permitted claims</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Beneficial effects should occur at typical dietary intake levels; EFSA evaluates function and risk‑reduction claims</cite>.

Caveats and how to avoid them
- Beware of “health halo” marketing: not every nutrient‑fortified product or food with “bioactive” sounding branding is evidence‑based; use EFSA/FDA‑authorized claims and look for biomarker changes and randomized‑trial evidence <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Marketing often uses health claims; various national/international bodies regulate their use and rigorous evaluation is required before marketing</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">EFSA distinguishes claim types and enforces scientific evaluation</cite>. 
- Consider interactions and safety: effective doses must be non‑toxic; toxicity and excess‑intake risks are part of the evaluation framework for bioactives and supplements <cite id="2faceea1-1">Definition emphasizes defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts and clinically proven benefits</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Regulatory frameworks cover bioavailability, clinical effect, permitted nutrition and health claims, and safety</cite>. 
- Recognize heterogeneity and individual variability: bioavailability, metabolism, and gut microbiota can determine whether a bioactive reaches active forms at dietary doses, underscoring why biomarker‑based validation is central <cite id="2faceea1-0">Bioactive compounds are heterogeneous with diverse health‑promoting properties; they are keystones for functional food development</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Clinical effect and bioavailability are key variables in regulatory frameworks</cite>.

Summary
- Food bioactives are non‑nutritive, naturally occurring food constituents that exert biological activity in humans beyond energy and macronutrient roles, often via antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, lipid‑lowering, and gene‑regulatory mechanisms, and can be harnessed in functional foods when effects are demonstrated with biomarkers and safety at realistic intakes; internationally, these effects are framed and regulated through health‑claims systems like EFSA’s, which evaluate physiological effects and disease‑risk impacts rather than prescribing a single universal definition of “functional food” <cite id="be6826b9-2">Food bioactives are extra‑nutritional, naturally occurring compounds associated with health changes</cite> <cite id="be6826b9-2">Mechanisms include inflammation modulation, lipid reduction, and gene regulation</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-1">Defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts with clinically proven, biomarker‑based benefits</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">Functional foods are those that beneficially affect target functions beyond nutrition</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-0">EFSA authorizes health claims under EU regulation</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Regulatory frameworks vary and emphasize typical dietary intake, biomarkers, and safety</cite>.

Snippet: Apart from lifestyle changes and the consumption of dietary supplements, the consumption of functional foods can also reduce the risk of developing diseases. (p. S26, [8]). The first functional food regulation, called "foods for specified health uses" (FOSHU), was introduced in Japan in 1991 (Iwatani and Yamammoto, 2019). A new Japanese system called "foods with function claims" has become more flexible than FOSHU regarding health claims, the protocol for clinical studies, and the required results in 2015. - Chemical classes and sources: Naturally occurring plant and microbial metabolites (e.g., phenolics, carotenoids, fibers, oligosaccharides, pectins, and bioactive peptides) are typical examples; they are diverse and heterogeneous, with discovery of new molecules ongoing <cite id="2faceea1-0">Bioactive compounds occur naturally as plant and/or microbial metabolites; they are keystones for functional food development, with examples including organic acids, phytochemicals (phenolics, carotenoids), oligosaccharides, pectins, and bioactive peptides</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-4">Bioactive compounds are natural compounds capable of interacting with one or more components of living tissues and exerting a variety of effects; distinctions with dietary supplements, nutraceuticals, and functional foods are sometimes misinterpreted</cite>. 
- Interaction and target specificity: A bioactive is a compound capable of interacting with tissues and altering biological processes, distinguishing it from bulk nutrients by mechanism‑level effects on pathways or biomarkers <cite id="2faceea1-4">Bioactive compounds are natural compounds capable of interacting with one or more components of living tissues and exerting a variety of effects</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">Health claims describe the physiological effects of food components, supported by EFSA</cite>.

Distinctions and cautions
- Avoiding overreach: Not all bioactives are nutrients; not all nutrients are bioactives. Practical identification and evaluation criteria
- Ask four questions:
  1) Is it present in foods at measurable levels apart from basic nutrients? <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactives are non‑nutritive constituents naturally present in foods</cite>.
  2) Does it show biological activity in humans (e.g., antioxidant capacity, anti‑inflammatory signaling, lipid lowering, gene regulation) at realistic intakes? <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactives modulate inflammation, reduce lipids, regulate gene expression; roles linked to prevention of chronic disease</cite>.
  3) Is the effect linked to specific target functions with biomarker changes and clinically relevant outcomes at defined, effective, non‑toxic doses and typical dietary exposure? <cite id="2faceea1-1">Defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts with clinically proven, biomarker‑utilizing benefits</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Effects should occur at intake levels consistent with typical diet; EFSA evaluates functional and risk‑reduction health claims</cite>.
  4) Is the label evidence‑based and compliant with regulatory health‑claim standards (e.g., EFSA authorization), or at least framed as a plausible, testable mechanism rather than unqualified disease prevention/treatment? <cite id="d1bd4a9e-0">EFSA authorizes health claims; marketing of health effects requires EFSA recommendation</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">EFSA distinguishes function health and disease risk‑reduction claims under 1924/2006</cite>.

Illustrative subdomains
- Phenolics and carotenoids (antioxidants), fibers and prebiotic oligosaccharides/pectins (gut microbiota modulation), and bioactive peptides (biopeptides) are canonical examples, illustrating how structure (molecule class and conformation) enables bioactivity via absorption, metabolism, and interaction with receptors/genes <cite id="2faceea1-0">Phytochemicals (phenolics and carotenoids), oligosaccharides, pectins, and bioactive peptides exemplify functional compounds</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-0">Bioactive compounds are natural plant and microbial metabolites with antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, antifungal, antimicrobial, and antiviral properties</cite>.

Putting it together: a working definition
- In practice, a food bioactive is any non‑nutritive, naturally occurring constituent of foods (and sometimes dietary supplements) that interacts with human tissues or biological systems to produce a measurable, beneficial change in physiological function or disease risk at intakes achievable in normal diets, distinct from the effects required to meet nutritional needs; evaluation relies on mechanistic plausibility, biomarker‑based endpoints, clinical evidence, and safety at defined effective doses, and is framed within regulated health‑claims systems such as EFSA’s in the EU <cite id="be6826b9-2">Bioactive compounds are extra‑nutritional, naturally occurring substances associated with changes in health status</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-1">Bioactive compounds in defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts provide clinically proven, biomarker‑based health benefits</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">A food is functional if it beneficially affects one or more target functions beyond nutrition</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-0">EFSA authorizes health claims; EU regulation (432/2012) lists permitted claims</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Beneficial effects should occur at typical dietary intake levels; EFSA evaluates function and risk‑reduction claims</cite>.

Caveats and how to avoid them
- Beware of “health halo” marketing: not every nutrient‑fortified product or food with “bioactive” sounding branding is evidence‑based; use EFSA/FDA‑authorized claims and look for biomarker changes and randomized‑trial evidence <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Marketing often uses health claims; various national/international bodies regulate their use and rigorous evaluation is required before marketing</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">EFSA distinguishes claim types and enforces scientific evaluation</cite>. 
- Consider interactions and safety: effective doses must be non‑toxic; toxicity and excess‑intake risks are part of the evaluation framework for bioactives and supplements <cite id="2faceea1-1">Definition emphasizes defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts and clinically proven benefits</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Regulatory frameworks cover bioavailability, clinical effect, permitted nutrition and health claims, and safety</cite>. 
- Recognize heterogeneity and individual variability: bioavailability, metabolism, and gut microbiota can determine whether a bioactive reaches active forms at dietary doses, underscoring why biomarker‑based validation is central <cite id="2faceea1-0">Bioactive compounds are heterogeneous with diverse health‑promoting properties; they are keystones for functional food development</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Clinical effect and bioavailability are key variables in regulatory frameworks</cite>.

Summary
- Food bioactives are non‑nutritive, naturally occurring food constituents that exert biological activity in humans beyond energy and macronutrient roles, often via antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, lipid‑lowering, and gene‑regulatory mechanisms, and can be harnessed in functional foods when effects are demonstrated with biomarkers and safety at realistic intakes; internationally, these effects are framed and regulated through health‑claims systems like EFSA’s, which evaluate physiological effects and disease‑risk impacts rather than prescribing a single universal definition of “functional food” <cite id="be6826b9-2">Food bioactives are extra‑nutritional, naturally occurring compounds associated with health changes</cite> <cite id="be6826b9-2">Mechanisms include inflammation modulation, lipid reduction, and gene regulation</cite> <cite id="2faceea1-1">Defined, effective, non‑toxic amounts with clinically proven, biomarker‑based benefits</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-3">Functional foods are those that beneficially affect target functions beyond nutrition</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-0">EFSA authorizes health claims under EU regulation</cite> <cite id="d1bd4a9e-4">Regulatory frameworks vary and emphasize typical dietary intake, biomarkers, and safety</cite>.

Title: Sustainable Food Systems: The Case of Functional Compounds towards the Development of Clean Label Food Products
Snippet: The term functional or bioactive compound is used to denote a class of diverse molecules that possess biological activity. These compounds occur naturally as plant and/or microbial metabolites. They are part of the food chain, eliciting essential or nonessential properties [13,16]. The interest for functional compounds is constantly flourishing as an equally increasing number of studies proves or highlights their benefits to human health. These compounds are the tangible example of Hippocrates' saying "Let food be your medicine", as they manifest a plethora of health-promoting and -protective properties such as antioxidant activity, anti-inflammatory, antifungal, antimicrobial and antiviral, to name a few [18]. 

Foods containing bioactive compounds with recognizable health-promoting properties can be characterized as functional. The properties indicating that a component possesses a certain bioactivity include the management, prevention and treatment of diseases through triggering or manipulating certain mechanisms in the human organism [18]. Even though an official definition of functional foods has yet to be provided, in 2017, the Functional Food Center gave the following definition, "Natural or processed foods that contain known or unknown biologically-active compounds; which, in defined, effective, and non-toxic amounts, provide a clinically proven and documented health benefit for the prevention, management, or treatment of chronic diseases" [18]. Functional foods' market accounted for approximately 178 billion U.S. dollars in 2019, while this is estimated to reach 268 billion U.S. dollars by 2027 [19]. The market includes vitamins and minerals, dietary fibers, probiotics, prebiotics, proteins and amino acids.

Snippet: The concept of functional foods has become increasingly popular in recent years (13)(14)(15), as people have become more health-conscious and seek ways to improve their well-being.Doyon and Labrecque (16) proposed the following definition of functional foods through literature review and Delphi method with experts: "A functional food is, or appears similar to, a conventional food.It is part of a standard diet and is consumed on a regular basis, in normal quantities.It has proven health benefits that reduce the risk of specific chronic diseases or beneficially affect target functions beyond its basic nutritional functions."

Additionally, functional foods are also considered to provide additional health benefits beyond basic nutrition (13).Health claims are often used in the marketing of these types of foods (17)(18)(19), as they highlight the potential health benefits and can influence consumer behavior (20).

Health claims are any statements or claims suggesting that a food has specific health benefits or can prevent or treat a disease (21,22).Health claims are used in packaging, advertising, and other promotional materials.Various national and international bodies regulate the use of health claims, including the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).In the European Union, health claims are subjected to a rigorous scientific evaluation process before they can be used in marketing (23).

Functional foods are often marketed using health claims, because these claims can help distinguish them from other types of food and therefore attract health-conscious consumers (24, 25).For example, products high in antioxidants may be marketed as having anti-aging properties (26), whereas those high in omega-3 fatty acids may be marketed as good for heart health (27).Health claims can also be used to differentiate between the different types of food within a category, such as between different types of yogurt or cereal.Another health claim strategy used in functional food advertisements is the use of scientific-sounding language.Food companies may use terms such as "clinically proven" or "scientifically tested" to give the impression that their products have been rigorously tested and proven effective (28).

Snippet: Apart from lifestyle changes and the consumption of dietary supplements, the consumption of functional foods can also reduce the risk of developing diseases. "A food can be regarded as 'functional' if it is satisfactorily demonstrated to affect beneficially one or more target functions in the body, beyond adequate nutritional effects in a way that is relevant to either an improved state of health and well-being and/or reduction of risk of disease." (p. S26, [8]). The different health claims manufacturers often use to communicate the positive effects of functional foods on health to consumers fall under European Food Safety Authority regulations. The specific regulation is included in regulation (EC) no. 1924/2006 [9]; the EFSA database makes all applicable health claims and nutrition claims available. The EFSA distinguishes different types of claims in the category of health claims, such as "Function health claims" (Article 13 claims), "Risk reduction claims" (Article 14(1)(a)), and "Claims referring to children's development" (Article 14(1)(b)) [10]. For the purposes of our research, one type of health claim, namely, risk reduction claims, are worth highlighting as they communicate the effect on the reduction of the risk of diseases [10]. 

In their research in Hungary, Szakály et al. came to the straightforward conclusion that "In the current situation, there is no other choice than to bring the public's attention to food products that possess an extra nutritional advantage" (p. 16, [11]). Owing to their ingredients, functional food products can help to prevent a variety of chronic diseases [12]. Encouragingly, several studies have indicated that due to increasing consumer concerns related to health, consumers would be willing to change their dietary habits and include products that would have a positive effect on their health in one way or another [13,14]. From the results of their focus group interviews, Szakály et al. concluded that if participants "have to choose between medication and functional food products, all of them would vote for the latter" (p. 23 [15]). 

Due to the complexities of developing functional foods, it is important to assess which diseases consumers are concerned about [16].

Title: Consumers’ attitudes and intentions toward functional beverages: a lesson for producers and retailers
Snippet: Functional food satisfactorily demonstrates to have a beneficial effect on one or more target functions in the body, beyond adequate nutritional effects, in a way that is relevant to either an improved state of physical, mental health, or both and well-being, a reduction in disease risk, or both (Birch and Bonwick 2019). However, there is no universal definition of functional food within the world: various countries have adopted different concepts in terms of definition and regulatory frameworks comprising the bioavailability of active ingredients, clinical effect, the permitted nutrition, health claims, and other relevant variables (Birch and Bonwick 2019). The lack of clarity on the definition has probably influenced consumer preferences and behavior in the functional food market and the efficiency of the marketing strategy developed by producers and retailers. 

The first functional food regulation, called "foods for specified health uses" (FOSHU), was introduced in Japan in 1991 (Iwatani and Yamammoto, 2019). A new Japanese system called "foods with function claims" has become more flexible than FOSHU regarding health claims, the protocol for clinical studies, and the required results in 2015. As a result, functional food sales in Japan started to rise sharply again (Iwatani and Yamamoto 2019). So far, a coherent regulatory framework for functional food has been lacking in the USA and the EU, but legislation on nutrition and health claims has been developed. As specified in Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 on nutrition and health claims made on foods, nutrition claims refer to what a food "contains" (nutrients or other substances) and "provides" (energy, caloric value), and health claims refer to what a food "does" in terms of human health. Three types of health claims, i.e., "function health claims," "risk reduction claims," and "claims referring to children's development," are often used by producers of functional foods. 

Functional beverages (FBs) are a very heterogeneous category, and there is a lack of classification of FBs in the literature.

A new Japanese system called "foods with function claims" has become more flexible than FOSHU regarding health claims, the protocol for clinical studies, and the required results in 2015. As a result, functional food sales in Japan started to rise sharply again (Iwatani and Yamamoto 2019). Three types of health claims, i.e., "function health claims," "risk reduction claims," and "claims referring to children's development," are often used by producers of functional foods. 

Functional beverages (FBs) are a very heterogeneous category, and there is a lack of classification of FBs in the literature.

attempts.answer:
Below are quantitative “thresholds” used in the literature to distinguish bioactive from non-bioactive food compounds. These thresholds are endpoint- and assay-specific: they commonly appear as analytical detection limits (LOD/LOQ), potency measures (IC50/EC50), exposure/bioavailability concentrations, or regulatory exposure thresholds (e.g., EFSA functional-claim standards). Where possible, I give numeric values, assay context, and the biological interpretation.

Scope and definitions
- Bioactivity is evaluated relative to an analytical endpoint (can the compound be measured reliably?), an in vitro or cellular effect (does it reach an EC50/IC50 or trigger a response?), an in vivo exposure/bioavailability level (does circulating concentration produce a physiological change?), and a regulatory exposure limit (is intake above levels that merit a health claim or safety review?). <cite id="dbb47113-0">Analytical sensitivity is often framed by limits of detection and quantification for phytochemicals in foods and supplements</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-0">In antioxidant testing, IC50 values and pragmatic categories are used to classify “effective” vs. “inactive” concentrations</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-0">Endogenous and dietary phenolics occur at low nanomolar–micromolar plasma levels yet can activate cytoprotective pathways via metabolites</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-4">Regulators like EFSA require specific physiological effects (e.g., raising HDL without raising LDL) and effective exposure ranges to substantiate functional health claims</cite>.

Analytical detection thresholds (LOD/LOQ) as practical bioactivity gatekeepers
- Many food-bioactive compound studies treat LOD/LOQ as the floor for “bioactivity”: below these, effects cannot be measured. Common S/N criteria are LOD at ~3:1 and LOQ at ~10:1; methods then report recoveries, linearity, and matrix-specific LOD/LOQ to ensure quantifiable concentrations in samples. <cite id="dbb47113-4">Calibration-line S/N ratios of 3:1 (LOD) and 10:1 (LOQ) are standard; LOD/LOQ are calculated from slope and residual variability and used to judge whether bioactive compounds are present at quantifiable levels</cite>. <cite id="dbb47113-0">Representative phenolic and flavonoid LODs/LOQ in ng/mL–µg/mL units (e.g., gallic acid LOD 41 ppb, LOQ 124 ppb; quercetin LOD 249 ppb, LOQ 756 ppb) illustrate typical sub-µg/mL quantification levels used to assess bioactives in complex food matrices</cite>. <cite id="dbb47113-2">Dietary supplement work similarly reports LOD/LOQ for menaquinone-7 alongside accuracy/precision to ensure that analyte levels can be measured above method noise</cite>.

In vitro potency thresholds and categorical IC50/EC50 cutoffs
- Antioxidant capacity: DPPH/ABTS and related assays convert EC50/IC50 into pragmatic categories. <cite id="9ff878b5-0">One widely used scheme classifies antioxidant extracts as very powerful when IC50 < 5 mg/mL, strong 50–100 µg/mL, moderate 101–250 µg/mL, weak 250–500 µg/mL, and inactive >500 µg/mL</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-1">A related categorization uses IC50 < 50 µg/mL as “very powerful,” with higher IC50 denoting decreasing activity; total phenolics/flavonoids correlate with lower IC50 in these readouts</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-3">For chamomile/water-immiscible systems, EC50 values of 0.59–3.08 mg·L−1 for hydrodistillate-derived residues indicate bioactivity at sub-mg/L levels in specific assay formats</cite>.
- Antimicrobial activity: Polyphenol-rich extracts often show low micromolar to sub-percent MIC/IC50 against foodborne pathogens; <cite id="9ff878b5-2">one study reported IC50 values “always below 3%” for a leaf extract with activity against Yersinia enterocolitica, Salmonella, and Listeria, whereas a petroleum-glycoside fraction required >10% extracts and higher MICs, showing assay- and solvent-dependent potency</cite>.
- General principle: lower IC50/EC50 implies stronger bioactivity; assay standards and controls contextualize “effective” vs. “ineffective.” <cite id="9ff878b5-0">Lower IC50 values indicate higher antioxidant activity for seed extracts across radical-scavenging methods (DPPH, ABTS), with trends aligned to phenolic richness</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-4">Across formulations, higher observed IC50 denotes weaker antioxidant strength, providing a direct numeric benchmark for potency gradients</cite>.

Exposure and bioavailability thresholds that translate intake to biological effect
- Plasma/metabolite levels: Phenolics often reach low nanomolar to micromolar plasma levels; metabolites (e.g., sulfates, glucuronides) may be biologically active and can exceed parent concentrations. <cite id="f814e655-0">Parent phenolic plasma concentrations of ~100 nM–10 µM are typical and not strongly shifted by phenolic-rich meals; metabolites can drive Nrf2/ARE-mediated antioxidant and cytoprotective responses despite modest parent levels</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-1">Hydroxytyrosol sulfates and other phenolic metabolites bind LDL and reinforce antioxidant action in vivo; phenolic-rich virgin olive oil increased LDL-bound metabolites and lowered lipid peroxidation markers in humans</cite>.
- Functional outcomes and serving thresholds: Epidemiologically relevant exposures can be quantified. <cite id="f814e655-3">Eight daily servings of fruits and vegetables significantly reduced plasma malondialdehyde (MDA) by ~0.15 mg/dL (p<0.05), while ≥5 servings lowered LDL-C in healthy young adults; prior RCTs reported 7–33% LDL-C reductions with plant-rich diets</cite>. These numeric intake thresholds link bioavailable phytochemicals and fibers to measurable cardiovascular risk biomarker changes.
- Specific polyphenol dose ranges for lipid effects: <cite id="f814e655-4">In olive oil polyphenols, daily intakes around 268–600 mg/kg body weight of phenols produced a significant ~4.28 mmol/L LDL-C reduction in meta-analysis, whereas pooled effects on TC and LDL were smaller and heterogeneous; olive oil polyphenols significantly raised HDL-C while not raising TC in aggregate</cite>. EFSA’s functional-claim criterion “improve HDL without increasing LDL” thus maps to these numeric exposure-response patterns.

Regulatory and claim thresholds: EFSA functional-claim standards and exposure benchmarks

Practical checklist for applying thresholds
- Can the compound be quantified in your matrix? Key takeaways
- Analytical thresholds: LOD/LOQ (often S/N 3:1/10:1) are the first gate for “bioactivity” in a study; below LOQ, biological effects cannot be reliably quantified. <cite id="dbb47113-4">LOD/LOQ criteria and calibration linearity underpin method sensitivity</cite>.

This concept would explain the relatively low concentrations of (poly)phenolics found in plasma (100 nM-10 μM), which is not dramatically affected by ingestion of phenolic-rich food [2,14,54]. The small amount of parent polyphenols that overcome the defence mechanism, together with the simple phenolic compounds that represent degradation products, imposes a mild noxious effect, driving Nrf-2/ARE-1-mediated upregulation of intracellular defence enzymes and xenobiotic-metabolising enzymes, leading to the observed antioxidant and cytoprotective effect.

In contradiction to common opinion, the protection offered does not appear to be related to direct antioxidant properties of the polyphenol itself; instead, modulation of intracellular defence mechanisms is a possible alternative mode of action. Moreover, this study suggests that degradation products are likely to be responsible for the observed biological activities, rather than the parent compound itself. This has profound implications for in vivo bioavailability studies, suggesting that our attention might have been previously misplaced and that we should instead measure phenolic metabolites, which can also confer bioactivity and might be present at concentrations higher than the parent compound(s). 

Dietary polyphenols have health-promoting qualities, but their mode of action still remains equivocal. A full understanding of the bioactive agents in vivo and their mode of action will help to shape public health advice. Title: Olive Oil Polyphenols Improve HDL Cholesterol and Promote Maintenance of Lipid Metabolism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
Snippet: This systematic review with a meta-analysis of human RCT studies evaluated the relationship between the daily consumption of olive oil polyphenols and HDL-C, LDL-C, and TC serum concentrations, to assess the existence of a positive effect on HDL-C without causing other lipid markers to alter for the worse, which is a specific criterion required by the EFSA to substantiate a functional health claim. The basic assumption is that HDL-C acts as a cholesterol scavenger and is involved in the reverse transport of cholesterol in the body, from peripheral tissues to the liver. In contrast, LDL transports cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues, including the arteries. The maintenance of normal HDL-C-without increasing LDL-C levels-is recognized as a beneficial physiological effect by the EFSA, while a functional claim would be granted to a food or substance able to exert this effect. 

Our findings showed that the daily consumption of olive oil polyphenols had no significant effect on TC levels in a total sample of 969 people (WMD pooled effect model 0.49, 95%CI −0.55 to 1.53, heterogeneity 14%, p = 0.28). Below are quantitative “thresholds” used in the literature to distinguish bioactive from non-bioactive food compounds. These thresholds are endpoint- and assay-specific: they commonly appear as analytical detection limits (LOD/LOQ), potency measures (IC50/EC50), exposure/bioavailability concentrations, or regulatory exposure thresholds (e.g., EFSA functional-claim standards). Where possible, I give numeric values, assay context, and the biological interpretation.

Scope and definitions
- Bioactivity is evaluated relative to an analytical endpoint (can the compound be measured reliably?), an in vitro or cellular effect (does it reach an EC50/IC50 or trigger a response?), an in vivo exposure/bioavailability level (does circulating concentration produce a physiological change?), and a regulatory exposure limit (is intake above levels that merit a health claim or safety review?). <cite id="dbb47113-0">Analytical sensitivity is often framed by limits of detection and quantification for phytochemicals in foods and supplements</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-0">In antioxidant testing, IC50 values and pragmatic categories are used to classify “effective” vs. “inactive” concentrations</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-0">Endogenous and dietary phenolics occur at low nanomolar–micromolar plasma levels yet can activate cytoprotective pathways via metabolites</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-4">Regulators like EFSA require specific physiological effects (e.g., raising HDL without raising LDL) and effective exposure ranges to substantiate functional health claims</cite>.

Analytical detection thresholds (LOD/LOQ) as practical bioactivity gatekeepers
- Many food-bioactive compound studies treat LOD/LOQ as the floor for “bioactivity”: below these, effects cannot be measured. Common S/N criteria are LOD at ~3:1 and LOQ at ~10:1; methods then report recoveries, linearity, and matrix-specific LOD/LOQ to ensure quantifiable concentrations in samples. <cite id="dbb47113-4">Calibration-line S/N ratios of 3:1 (LOD) and 10:1 (LOQ) are standard; LOD/LOQ are calculated from slope and residual variability and used to judge whether bioactive compounds are present at quantifiable levels</cite>. <cite id="dbb47113-0">Representative phenolic and flavonoid LODs/LOQ in ng/mL–µg/mL units (e.g., gallic acid LOD 41 ppb, LOQ 124 ppb; quercetin LOD 249 ppb, LOQ 756 ppb) illustrate typical sub-µg/mL quantification levels used to assess bioactives in complex food matrices</cite>. <cite id="dbb47113-2">Dietary supplement work similarly reports LOD/LOQ for menaquinone-7 alongside accuracy/precision to ensure that analyte levels can be measured above method noise</cite>.

In vitro potency thresholds and categorical IC50/EC50 cutoffs
- Antioxidant capacity: DPPH/ABTS and related assays convert EC50/IC50 into pragmatic categories. <cite id="9ff878b5-0">One widely used scheme classifies antioxidant extracts as very powerful when IC50 < 5 mg/mL, strong 50–100 µg/mL, moderate 101–250 µg/mL, weak 250–500 µg/mL, and inactive >500 µg/mL</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-1">A related categorization uses IC50 < 50 µg/mL as “very powerful,” with higher IC50 denoting decreasing activity; total phenolics/flavonoids correlate with lower IC50 in these readouts</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-3">For chamomile/water-immiscible systems, EC50 values of 0.59–3.08 mg·L−1 for hydrodistillate-derived residues indicate bioactivity at sub-mg/L levels in specific assay formats</cite>.
- Antimicrobial activity: Polyphenol-rich extracts often show low micromolar to sub-percent MIC/IC50 against foodborne pathogens; <cite id="9ff878b5-2">one study reported IC50 values “always below 3%” for a leaf extract with activity against Yersinia enterocolitica, Salmonella, and Listeria, whereas a petroleum-glycoside fraction required >10% extracts and higher MICs, showing assay- and solvent-dependent potency</cite>.
- General principle: lower IC50/EC50 implies stronger bioactivity; assay standards and controls contextualize “effective” vs. “ineffective.” <cite id="9ff878b5-0">Lower IC50 values indicate higher antioxidant activity for seed extracts across radical-scavenging methods (DPPH, ABTS), with trends aligned to phenolic richness</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-4">Across formulations, higher observed IC50 denotes weaker antioxidant strength, providing a direct numeric benchmark for potency gradients</cite>.

Exposure and bioavailability thresholds that translate intake to biological effect
- Plasma/metabolite levels: Phenolics often reach low nanomolar to micromolar plasma levels; metabolites (e.g., sulfates, glucuronides) may be biologically active and can exceed parent concentrations. <cite id="f814e655-0">Parent phenolic plasma concentrations of ~100 nM–10 µM are typical and not strongly shifted by phenolic-rich meals; metabolites can drive Nrf2/ARE-mediated antioxidant and cytoprotective responses despite modest parent levels</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-1">Hydroxytyrosol sulfates and other phenolic metabolites bind LDL and reinforce antioxidant action in vivo; phenolic-rich virgin olive oil increased LDL-bound metabolites and lowered lipid peroxidation markers in humans</cite>.
- Functional outcomes and serving thresholds: Epidemiologically relevant exposures can be quantified. <cite id="f814e655-3">Eight daily servings of fruits and vegetables significantly reduced plasma malondialdehyde (MDA) by ~0.15 mg/dL (p<0.05), while ≥5 servings lowered LDL-C in healthy young adults; prior RCTs reported 7–33% LDL-C reductions with plant-rich diets</cite>. These numeric intake thresholds link bioavailable phytochemicals and fibers to measurable cardiovascular risk biomarker changes.
- Specific polyphenol dose ranges for lipid effects: <cite id="f814e655-4">In olive oil polyphenols, daily intakes around 268–600 mg/kg body weight of phenols produced a significant ~4.28 mmol/L LDL-C reduction in meta-analysis, whereas pooled effects on TC and LDL were smaller and heterogeneous; olive oil polyphenols significantly raised HDL-C while not raising TC in aggregate</cite>. EFSA’s functional-claim criterion “improve HDL without increasing LDL” thus maps to these numeric exposure-response patterns.

Regulatory and claim thresholds: EFSA functional-claim standards and exposure benchmarks
- EFSA requires reproducible physiological effects and appropriate exposure to justify functional health claims. <cite id="f814e655-4">For olive oil polyphenols, meta-analysis showed that raising HDL-C and lowering LDL-C can be achieved simultaneously without increasing total cholesterol at effective daily intakes of approximately 268–600 mg/kg of olive oil polyphenols, satisfying EFSA’s “specific criterion” for granting a functional claim</cite>. While thresholds are compound- and function-specific, this provides a concrete numeric exemplar for “biologically effective exposure” in EU regulation.
- More generally, EFSA’s “biological effect” assessments hinge on NOAEL/BOEL-like boundaries; when bioactive metabolites or metabolites exceed method noise and produce in vivo effect sizes at feasible intakes, EFSA deems claims substantiated. <cite id="f814e655-1">Clinical data linking phenolic metabolites to reduced LDL peroxidation markers and increased HDL provide the exposure-effect evidence EFSA requires for claim substantiation</cite>.

Compound-class examples and their characteristic numeric thresholds
- Polyphenols/anthocyanins: <cite id="f814e655-0">Berry-derived phenolics at sub-µM to low-hundred-nM plasma levels can activate Nrf2/ARE pathways via metabolites, indicating biological activity despite low parent concentrations</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-2">Anthocyanins show low systemic bioavailability in humans and animals; metabolites appear in plasma 1–2 hours post intake, yet overall systemic concentrations remain limited, affecting the magnitude of biological effects</cite>.
- Olive oil phenols: <cite id="f814e655-4">Effective exposure ranges of roughly 268–600 mg/kg/day of olive oil phenolic compounds are associated with significant LDL-C lowering while increasing HDL-C, aligning with EFSA’s functional-claim standard for “improves HDL-C without increasing LDL-C”</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-1">Dose-dependent increases in LDL-associated phenolic metabolites and parallel reductions in circulating lipid peroxidation markers provide causal links between exposure and effect</cite>.
- Plant-rich diets (fiber + polyphenols): <cite id="f814e655-3">Practical dietary thresholds emerge from trials: ≥5 servings/day reduce LDL-C, and ≥8 servings/day reduce MDA by ~0.15 mg/dL; reductions scale with phenolic/fiber content across studies</cite>.
- Antimicrobial polyphenols/extracts: <cite id="9ff878b5-2">IC50 values below 3% (w/v) demonstrate potent bacteriostasis against Salmonella enterica and other foodborne pathogens, whereas higher-solvent extracts show IC50 >10% and higher MICs, underscoring solvent and matrix effects on potency thresholds</cite>.

Putting the thresholds together: how to judge “bioactive vs. non-bioactive”
- Below LOD/LOQ: Not bioactive for study purposes. <cite id="dbb47113-4">Assay LOD/LOQ (S/N 3:1/10:1) set the floor for reliable detection; concentrations below LOQ cannot be quantified and thus cannot be tied to dose–response effects</cite>.
- In vitro potency: Use IC50/EC50 benchmarks for the assay. <cite id="9ff878b5-0">IC50 < 5 mg/mL often denotes “very powerful” antioxidant in DPPH/ABTS-type screens; higher IC50 denotes weaker activity and “inactive” above ~500 µg/mL–5 mg/mL depending on scheme</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-1">An alternative categorization labels IC50 < 50 µg/mL as “very powerful,” providing a consistent numeric ladder for comparing extracts</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-2">For antimicrobial activity, sub-3% IC50 indicates strong activity against key foodborne pathogens in certain extracts, while >10% suggests limited potency</cite>.
- In vivo relevance: Bioavailability and metabolite levels must exceed noise and produce physiological changes at feasible intakes. <cite id="f814e655-0">Parent phenolics are often nanomolar–micromolar in plasma, but metabolites can be bioactive and drive pathway activation</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-3">≥5–8 daily servings of fruits/vegetables can shift LDL oxidation and LDL-C by clinically meaningful amounts</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-4">Olive oil polyphenols at ~268–600 mg/kg/day reduce LDL-C and raise HDL-C in meta-analyzed RCTs, matching EFSA functional-claim criteria</cite>.
- Regulatory framing: Intake ranges that produce consistent benefits without unacceptable adverse effects are the practical “upper bound” of non-harmful bioactivity for functional claims. <cite id="f814e655-4">EFSA grants claims when effects (e.g., HDL up, LDL unchanged/low) are reproducible in pooled RCTs at defined exposure levels; numeric meta-analytic dose–response estimates define effective thresholds for specific compounds</cite>.

Practical checklist for applying thresholds
- Can the compound be quantified in your matrix? If below LOQ (S/N <10:1), consider co-extractions, fractionation, or alternative methods. <cite id="dbb47113-0">Phenolics and flavonoids often require sub-µg/mL quantification in foods</cite>. <cite id="dbb47113-4">Design assays to meet LOD/LOQ criteria and validate linearity and recovery</cite>.
- Does it show in vitro potency at your target pathway? Benchmark to known IC50/EC50 ranges for your assay and compound class to classify “active vs. inactive.” <cite id="9ff878b5-0">IC50 categories provide pragmatic cutoffs for antioxidant strength</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-2">MIC/IC50 against pathogens give antimicrobial potency thresholds</cite>.
- Will exposure in vivo exceed bioactivity-relevant levels? Consider parent vs. metabolite concentrations and dietary thresholds that reproduce biological endpoints. <cite id="f814e655-0">Metabolite-driven cytoprotection at low nanomolar–micromolar levels is possible</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-3">≥5–8 servings/day of fruits/vegetables shift lipid oxidative stress markers and LDL-C</cite>.
- Does intake evidence meet regulatory standards? For functional claims, show consistent RCT effects at feasible intakes and define dose ranges. <cite id="f814e655-4">Olive oil polyphenols at ~268–600 mg/kg/day lower LDL-C without raising TC and increase HDL-C, satisfying EFSA’s criteria for claim substantiation</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Analytical thresholds: LOD/LOQ (often S/N 3:1/10:1) are the first gate for “bioactivity” in a study; below LOQ, biological effects cannot be reliably quantified. <cite id="dbb47113-4">LOD/LOQ criteria and calibration linearity underpin method sensitivity</cite>.
- Potency thresholds: IC50/EC50 benchmarks and categorical ranges (e.g., DPPH/ABTS IC50 < 5–50 µg/mL as “very powerful,” sub-3% for antimicrobial IC50) operationalize in vitro bioactivity. <cite id="9ff878b5-0">IC50 categories classify effect strength</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-2">Sub-3% IC50 indicates strong antibacterial activity in certain extracts</cite>.
- Exposure thresholds: Plasma/metabolite levels and dietary intakes must produce physiological changes; nanomolar–micromolar metabolites can be bioactive, while diets of ≥5–8 servings/day and specific polyphenol intakes can significantly modulate lipid profiles and oxidative stress. <cite id="f814e655-0">Metabolites drive cytoprotection at low levels</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-3">Fruit/vegetable intake of ≥5–8 servings/day changes LDL and MDA</cite>. <cite id="f814e655-4">Olive oil polyphenols at ~268–600 mg/kg/day reduce LDL and raise HDL in meta-analyzed trials</cite>.
- Regulatory thresholds: EFSA-style functional-claim thresholds require reproducible physiological effects at feasible intakes; numeric pooled-effect estimates define effective exposure ranges for specific compounds. <cite id="f814e655-4">Meta-analyses provide concrete dose–response ranges to substantiate claims</cite>.

Caveats and variability
- Thresholds are highly assay- and matrix-specific. <cite id="9ff878b5-2">Solvent and extraction conditions shift IC50/MIC by an order of magnitude or more</cite>. <cite id="9ff878b5-3">Total phenolic content does not always correlate linearly with antioxidant EC50, underscoring the need for direct potency assays</cite>. <cite id="dbb47113-0">LOD/LOQ depend on matrix effects and chromatographic response, requiring validation in each food system</cite>. Consequently, “bioactive” should be interpreted as “dose–response effective at a defined assay endpoint and exposure level,” not a universal numeric cutoff across all contexts.
</answer>

Therefore, the extensive metabolism that they are exposed to, coupled with their low bioavailability, may be a result of the natural defence against a potentially toxic insult. This concept would explain the relatively low concentrations of (poly)phenolics found in plasma (100 nM-10 μM), which is not dramatically affected by ingestion of phenolic-rich food [2,14,54]. The small amount of parent polyphenols that overcome the defence mechanism, together with the simple phenolic compounds that represent degradation products, imposes a mild noxious effect, driving Nrf-2/ARE-1-mediated upregulation of intracellular defence enzymes and xenobiotic-metabolising enzymes, leading to the observed antioxidant and cytoprotective effect. 

The results of this study provide support for the view that delphindin-and potentially other berry-derived polyphenols-has the capability to protect endothelial cells against oxidative stress, perhaps via an indirect route. In contradiction to common opinion, the protection offered does not appear to be related to direct antioxidant properties of the polyphenol itself; instead, modulation of intracellular defence mechanisms is a possible alternative mode of action. Moreover, this study suggests that degradation products are likely to be responsible for the observed biological activities, rather than the parent compound itself. This has profound implications for in vivo bioavailability studies, suggesting that our attention might have been previously misplaced and that we should instead measure phenolic metabolites, which can also confer bioactivity and might be present at concentrations higher than the parent compound(s). 

Dietary polyphenols have health-promoting qualities, but their mode of action still remains equivocal. A full understanding of the bioactive agents in vivo and their mode of action will help to shape public health advice. There are also profound consequences of our findings for research practice, particularly with respect to the relevance of in vitro antioxidant (reducing capacity) testing as an indication of putative health benefits of food extracts or polyphenolic compounds.

Title: The Benefits of Anthocyanins against Obesity-Induced Inflammation
Snippet: The majority of bioactive compounds in functional foods have been linked to lower risks of chronic conditions including CVD and T2DM [8]. Examinations of plasma after intake of anthocyanin-rich foods such as blackcurrant juice, red wine, and strawberries, have revealed that anthocyanins have limited bioavailability in humans as well [26][27][28]. Title: Olive Oil Polyphenols Improve HDL Cholesterol and Promote Maintenance of Lipid Metabolism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
Snippet: This systematic review with a meta-analysis of human RCT studies evaluated the relationship between the daily consumption of olive oil polyphenols and HDL-C, LDL-C, and TC serum concentrations, to assess the existence of a positive effect on HDL-C without causing other lipid markers to alter for the worse, which is a specific criterion required by the EFSA to substantiate a functional health claim. The basic assumption is that HDL-C acts as a cholesterol scavenger and is involved in the reverse transport of cholesterol in the body, from peripheral tissues to the liver. In contrast, LDL transports cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues, including the arteries. The maintenance of normal HDL-C-without increasing LDL-C levels-is recognized as a beneficial physiological effect by the EFSA, while a functional claim would be granted to a food or substance able to exert this effect. 

Our findings showed that the daily consumption of olive oil polyphenols had no significant effect on TC levels in a total sample of 969 people (WMD pooled effect model 0.49, 95%CI −0.55 to 1.53, heterogeneity 14%, p = 0.28). However, when LDL-C was targeted, the daily consumption of olive oil polyphenols slightly but significantly reduced LDL-C levels in a total sample of 991 people (WMDs common effect model −0.83, 95%CI −1.67 to 0.01, heterogeneity 73%, p < 0.01), and the WMDs for each daily exposure level showed a strong significant effect on LDL-C reduction but only following a high daily consumption (268-600 mg/kg) of olive oil polyphenols (WMD −4.28, 95%CI −5.78 to −2.77). Interestingly, HDL-C levels were found to be significantly enhanced in a total sample of 991 subjects (WMD pooled effect model 1.13, 95%CI 0.45; 1.80, heterogeneity 38%, p = 0.04).
